rewriteLast.title: Chapter 6 · The White Knight
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a kindly old knight in rusty armour riding a shaggy horse piled with straps and boxes, a girl in a blue dress walking beside him in a mossy wood, the knight tipping sideways in his saddle, golden evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Alice went on toward the Eighth Square, and soon she heard hoofs thundering in the wood. A Red Knight came riding at her and pulled up close. "You are my prisoner!" he cried. Before Alice could answer, a second horse came galloping. A White Knight had ridden up on the other side. He called out in a kind voice that the little girl was under his protection.
The White Knight rides to Alice's rescue through the golden wood.

Then the two knights rode at each other to fight. They held their sticks upside down, and they held on tight to their horses. Blow after blow they gave each other, till Alice trembled to watch. At last the Red Knight tumbled from his saddle and sat down in the bracken. The White Knight calmly put his helmet on again, as if nothing at all had happened.

The White Knight was a very odd old gentleman. His armour was rusty, and his horse was slung with straps and boxes and bundles. Still, he could not sit on his horse to save his life. He fell off backwards, then sideways, then head first. He never minded. He just picked himself up and offered Alice his arm, as politely as if he had done it on purpose.
New word: armour — the metal suit that knights wore to keep themselves safe in battle.

He told Alice all about his inventions. He had made metal anklets to keep his horse safe from shark bites. He had made a great box to carry clothes and puddings, all mixed up together. Then he sang her a long, mournful song about an aged, aged man who sat upon a gate. Alice said it was very beautiful. "It is very long, too," said the Knight, and looked pleased.

At the last brook of all, the Knight lifted Alice gently across. "Good-bye, little Alice," he said. "You will be a Queen before you know it." She watched him ride slowly away, until he was only a little dot on the hillside. Then she turned and stepped on, quite alone, into the Eighth Square.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Queen Alice
chapters.artPrompt: a golden crown settling on the hair of a girl in a blue dress, a Red Chess Queen and a White Chess Queen in red and white gowns gliding up on either side of her, a green hillock on a black-and-white chequered meadow, bright noon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Something glittered above Alice's head. She put up her hand, and there sat a golden crown, tall and heavy, in her hair. "I really am a Queen at last!" she cried, and sat down on a soft green hillock. Then two Queens came gliding silently up, one on each side of her. They were the Red Queen and the White Queen.
The Red Queen and the White Queen greet Alice, crowned Queen of the chessboard.

The Red Queen began to ask sharp questions at once. "What do you mean by coming here without an invitation? Can you do addition? What is one and one and one and one and one and one?" "I don't know," said Alice. "I lost count." "She can't do addition," said the Red Queen sorrowfully. "Can you do subtraction? Take nine from eight." "Nine from eight I can't, you know," said Alice. And the Red Queen looked as if she could not do subtraction either.

The White Queen was kinder, but very odd too. "When I was your age," she said, "I always did things for half an hour a day. Why, sometimes I have believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast!" Then the two Queens began to tidy Alice all over. They smoothed her hair and pinned her with great silver pins, till she could hardly move.
Question for you: The White Queen believes six impossible things before breakfast. What is the most impossible thing you could try to believe today?

Alice stood up and shook herself free. "You are not Queens at all," she said. "You are two fussy old women!" But she took an arm of each Queen, and off they went through the meadow. They went faster and faster, all the way to the great castle of the Eighth Square. The Red Queen grew deafer at every step, and made Alice shout.

At the castle gates the two Queens suddenly vanished, crowns and all. Alice stood quite alone before a long, long table, spread with silver dishes and lit by tall white candles. A tall chair waited at the head. "I suppose I must be the hostess," said Alice, and sat down, feeling very grand and rather frightened.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Queen's Feast
chapters.artPrompt: a long banquet table with silver dishes and tall white candles, a girl in a blue dress standing up on a chair at the head, a candle growing taller and taller toward the ceiling, chess queens and lords in red and white, warm candlelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Alice had meant to introduce all her guests, but the harder she tried, the more she forgot. "Never mind," she said at last. "They can be introduced to me." Then the Red Queen called out, "Let me introduce you to the leg of mutton." And the leg of mutton rose in its silver dish and made a little bow. "May I give you a slice?" asked Alice, taking up the knife and fork. "Certainly not," said the Red Queen. "It isn't etiquette to cut anyone you have been introduced to."
At the royal feast, even the leg of mutton stands up and bows.

The dishes were very grand, and the candles were the tallest Alice had ever seen. But the feast would not keep quiet. The great candle above Alice's head grew taller and taller, till it brushed the ceiling. The dishes slid and clattered, and the guests rose up in their places. The Red Queen talked nonsense louder and louder. Alice stood up on her chair. "I can't stand this any longer!" she cried.

She seized the table-cloth with both hands, and gave one good, sharp pull. Down came plates, dishes, candles, guests and all, in one tremendous heap on the floor. The great candle went out, and the room was dark for a moment. Only the Red Queen sat quite still among the wreck. And that was more than Alice could bear.
Question for you: What would you do if the candle grew taller and the dishes began to walk about at your dinner?

She seized the Red Queen with both hands and shook her, backwards and forwards, with all her might. "Beware in time!" The Queen's voice grew thin, like wind in the reeds. But the Queen's face grew smaller and smaller in Alice's hands, till it was hardly bigger than a doll's. And then it was not a Queen's face at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Black Kitten
chapters.artPrompt: a girl in a blue dress by a bright fire holding a small black kitten in her lap, tangled loops of red and blue wool lying on the rug, scattered chess pieces, a tall mirror glowing faintly above the fireplace, cosy evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Alice opened her eyes. She was back in the big arm-chair by the fire. The black kitten was sitting in her lap, blinking at her with round green eyes. "So it was you all the time!" cried Alice. "You played the Red Queen, and played her very well, Kitty - though you were rather cross to me sometimes."
In Alice's hands the Red Queen dwindles into a small black kitten.

The wool lay about the rug in bright, tangled loops. Alice gathered up a ball of worsted and began to unwind it, carefully, turn by turn. The kitten purred all the while, as if it had done nothing wrong at all. "And you, Snowdrop," she said to the white kitten, who had crept up to see, "you were the White Queen. But you slept through the whole game, I am sure."
New word: worsted — soft wool thread, spun for knitting. The kitten thought it was made for playing with.

"If you don't mind," said Alice, "tomorrow shall be a washing-day for both of you. Dinah shall wash your faces, and make you clean all over." The kittens said nothing at all, for cats do not like to be talked to about washing. But their eyes shone green in the firelight, and Alice was quite sure that they were smiling.

Alice pulled her chair closer to the fire and tucked the rug round her knees. Outside, the winter garden was dark and still, and the last leaves rattled on the path. Inside, all was warm, and quiet, and safe.

At last the wool was wound and tidy, and the fire was only a little heap of red coals. Alice looked up at the mirror over the fireplace, and nodded to it politely. "Thank you for the game," she whispered. And the glass seemed to glitter a little, like water when the sun touches it.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Red King's Dream
chapters.artPrompt: a red-bearded chess king in a red gown fast asleep under a spreading tree on a black-and-white chequered meadow, a girl in a blue dress watching him from a distance among whispering trees, deep dusk light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The room was very quiet, and Alice sat on with a kitten on each side of her. She told them all about the chessboard world. "The strangest part of all is about the Red King," she said. "He was asleep under his tree the whole time. He was dreaming the whole game - knights and Queens and castles, and me as well."
Far away on the chequered meadow, the Red King sleeps and dreams under his tree.

She thought of the Red King lying on the grass, with his red gown spread about him. His dream had gone on all through the game, quiet as a stream. It had carried her, and the Queens, and the whole board, from square to square. And he never turned once in his sleep.

"And if he was dreaming me," said Alice, "then when he wakes up, I shall go out like a candle! But if I was dreaming him, then it is I who must not wake too soon." The Red King's own dream, she thought, going on and on under the tree, like a river in the night.

She looked gravely at the two little cats. "Either I dreamed the Red King, or the Red King is dreaming me. And I don't see how anyone in the world could ever find out which it was." It was the strangest question she had ever asked. And there was no one to answer it but two sleepy kittens.
Question for you: Alice says either she dreamed the Red King, or the Red King is dreaming her. Which do you think it was - and how could anyone ever be sure?

The kittens purred and purred, and the winter stars came out over the white garden. Alice's eyes grew heavy. She nestled her chin into their soft fur, and half closed her eyes. And she let the dream take her gently by the hand. Very soon she was fast asleep, with the kittens rising and falling with her breath.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · A Story on the River
chapters.artPrompt: an old wooden rowing-boat drifting on a green and golden river in high summer, a girl in a blue dress telling a story to her two little sisters among the cushions, willow boughs trailing over the water, warm afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long, long after that winter evening, there came a golden summer afternoon. Alice sat in a rowing-boat on the river, with her sisters on the cushions beside her. The water slid past, green and shining, and the banks were full of meadow-sweet and tall grasses. Far away, a cuckoo was calling across the meadows.

As they passed under a willow tree, a loose bough caught Alice's hair. She laughed, and put it back, and lay still in the bottom of the boat. She looked up at the blue sky. Her sisters made room for her among the cushions. Then she began to tell them a story. It was a wonderful story about a girl who climbed through a mirror into a chessboard land.
On a golden afternoon, a drifting rowing-boat carries Alice and her sisters down the shining river.

The little sisters had asked for this story many times. But this golden afternoon was the very first telling of it. The water chuckled under the bow. The story went with the boat, from bend to bend of the river, like a happy secret.

She told them about the garden of talking flowers, and the twins under the tree. She told them about the great egg on the wall. She told them about the Lion and the Unicorn, and the kind old Knight who fell off his horse. She told them about the two Queens who vanished at the gates. Nobody moved, for fear the story should stop.
New word: meadow-sweet — a tall plant with little cream-coloured flowers, that grows by rivers.

The story was long, but nobody wanted it to stop. "And then what happened?" the smallest sister kept asking. And Alice would smile, and think, and go on. The sun sank lower, and the river turned from green to gold. The shadows of the willows lay long across the water.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Which Dreamed It?
chapters.artPrompt: a small rowing-boat slipping through gold and rose twilight on a quiet river, a girl in a blue dress and two little sisters looking up at the first star, willow shadows lying long across the water, soft fading light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The shadows grew long, and the sky turned gold and rose. At last the smallest sister sat up among the cushions. "Alice," she asked gravely, "which of all of it was a dream? Was the looking-glass world true, or did somebody dream it? Was the Red Queen real? And the White Knight?"

Her sisters thought about it very hard, as children do. "Then we might be in somebody's dream this very minute," said the middle sister. "And somebody might be dreaming us," said the eldest. The boat rocked, and the idea rocked with it. The oars lay still in the water, and the boat drifted where it liked.

Alice looked down the long river, shining away into the west. "Either I dreamed the Red King," she said, "or the Red King dreamed me. And which of it was a dream, and which of it was true - nobody can ever tell." She smiled a little. "Life, what is it but a dream?"
In the gold and rose twilight, the little boat slips quietly on down the shining river.

Nobody spoke for a while after that. The boat slipped softly on, under the willows, into the twilight. The water whispered under the bow, and the first star came out, small and clear, above the dark trees. Far off in a field, a nightingale began to sing.
Question for you: On the river, Alice tells her sisters about the Red King's dream. Would you like a dream that goes on and on, or a dream that ends when you wake up?

And so the story ends, as all the best stories do. It ends gently, in the summer twilight, with the river still going on. But somewhere, the children felt quite sure, the looking-glass still glitters above a quiet fire. And the chess people are playing still. So good-night to all the chess people, gently and kindly, wherever they may be playing. And perhaps, some night, they dream of us - just as we dream of them.
